items.quote: So the messengers returned and reported to the king. Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Arameans.
items.contrast: The messengers’ return and report is the immediately preceding event; following the Arameans toward the Jordan occurs earlier.
items.reason: The explicit sequence resolves the plausible confusion between an earlier pursuit and the event directly before the plundering.

items.quote: They piled them against the stronghold and set it on fire with the people still inside. So all the people in the tower of Shechem, about a thousand men and women, also died.
items.contrast: Entering the stronghold places the people inside, whereas the fire is what kills them.
items.reason: The passage directly links setting the occupied stronghold on fire with the occupants’ deaths.

items.quote: Then Jotham fled, escaping to Beer, and he lived there because he was afraid of his brother Abimelek.
items.contrast: Jotham lives in Beer because he fears Abimelek, not the citizens of Shechem mentioned later.
items.reason: The causal answer is explicit and unique, but “elsewhere” is an avoidable vague substitute for Beer. Asking why Jotham lived in Beer would be clearer.

items.quote: He had people working his fields and vineyards in the hills and in the fertile lands, for he loved the soil.
items.contrast: The singular owner, Uzziah, loves the soil; the people are those he has working his land.
items.reason: The pronouns continue to refer to Uzziah, the passage’s singular subject, rather than to the plural workers.

items.quote: If you have, may Abimelek be your joy, and may you be his, too! But if you have not, let fire come out from Abimelek and consume you
items.contrast: The preceding conditional wish is for mutual joy; the consumption by fire belongs to the following conditional curse.
items.reason: The sequence uniquely supports the key, but “request” inaccurately labels a conditional wish or blessing. Asking what wish is expressed before the call for fire would be clearer.
